paragraphs: The paper studies how to maintain a low-cost covering solution when available elements keep changing. In the classical problem, a monotone submodular function measures what a chosen set achieves, and the goal is to match the value of the entire available set at minimum cost. This formulation includes familiar problems such as set cover and dominating set.

The dynamic version allows elements to enter or leave the available set. An algorithm must therefore adjust its solution as the target and available choices change. The authors propose a randomized algorithm designed to maintain an approximately optimal solution while making relatively few queries after each update.

Its guarantee trades off coverage and cost: in expectation, it achieves a 1−O(ε) fraction of the target value with an O(1/ε) cost approximation. The number of queries per update is polylogarithmic. Thus, the contribution is an efficient maintenance guarantee that permits a controlled coverage shortfall, rather than requiring exact full coverage after every change.
icml-2024-a-dynamic-algorithm-for-weight.tldr: A randomized algorithm maintains approximately optimal submodular covers under insertions and deletions with polylogarithmic query complexity per update.

paragraphs: Advertising platforms often manage two related requirements: keeping spending within a budget and obtaining sufficient value for that spending. These requirements may be handled by separate pacing systems for historical or business reasons. The paper asks how much coordination those systems need to control both constraints effectively.

The authors compare three approaches: a fully separate sequential procedure, a minimally coordinated min-pacing procedure, and a fully coordinated method based on a joint dual formulation. Their main theoretical result shows that min-pacing achieves guarantees similar to those of the fully coordinated approach. By contrast, the sequential procedure can badly violate the constraints, despite its appealing separation of responsibilities.

Experiments on semi-synthetic data derived from an advertising platform’s auctions support the theoretical comparison: min-pacing performs almost as well as the fully coordinated method. The practical significance is that limited coordination can retain much of the benefit of joint optimization. Simply running independent controls in sequence, however, does not provide the same assurance.
icml-2024-a-field-guide-for-pacing-budge.tldr: Minimal coordination between budget and return-on-spend pacing can achieve guarantees similar to full coordination, while sequential independent controls can violate constraints.

paragraphs: Combinatorial bandit problems involve repeatedly choosing combinations of basic actions and learning from their outcomes. This paper studies reward poisoning, in which an adversary manipulates the reward information used for learning. The central question is which problem instances are vulnerable to this kind of interference.

The authors establish a condition that is both necessary and sufficient for attackability. It depends on properties of the instance, including reward distributions for combined actions and outcome distributions for basic actions. They also develop an attack algorithm for attackable instances. A key finding is that vulnerability depends additionally on whether the adversary knows the bandit instance.

This dependence on knowledge changes the practical interpretation of an attackability result: an attack that is possible with a known environment need not translate into a general strategy for an unknown one. Experiments involving probabilistic covering, spanning trees, online ranking, and shortest paths support the theory. The findings identify structure and adversary knowledge as distinct ingredients in understanding vulnerability.
icml-2024-adversarial-attacks-on-combina.tldr: The paper characterizes when combinatorial bandits are vulnerable to reward poisoning and shows that an adversary’s knowledge affects attackability.

paragraphs: A three-dimensional point cloud describes a collection of spatial locations, but it may arrive without a predefined reference frame. That creates an alignment problem before machine learning or other analysis can proceed. Existing approaches to choosing a frame can struggle with particular inputs, lack guarantees, or depend on large amounts of training data.

The paper introduces an explicit algorithm for constructing a frame and normalizing point clouds. The authors state that it works for any input point cloud and is compatible with any learnable framework for point-cloud analysis. This makes the frame construction a broadly applicable preparation step, rather than a procedure tied to one downstream model.

The contribution combines a universality guarantee with empirical comparisons across diverse benchmark datasets. Those comparisons show better effectiveness and generalizability than existing methods. Its significance is the combination of input coverage and model compatibility: the proposed normalization is intended to handle complicated inputs consistently without relying on a learned frame estimator whose behavior depends on its training data.
icml-2024-an-explicit-frame-construction.tldr: An explicit frame-construction algorithm normalizes arbitrary 3D point clouds with universality guarantees and compatibility across learnable analysis frameworks.

paragraphs: D^α seeding is a method for choosing initial cluster centers; its α=2 version is known as k-means++. Earlier experiments suggested that using α greater than two can improve the ordinary k-means objective, even though that objective still uses squared distances. This paper provides theoretical support for that observation.

The authors derive an expected approximation guarantee for every α greater than two. Its quality depends on how concentrated points are within clusters, how much cluster standard deviations differ, and how many distinct cluster mixing weights remain after rounding. The result therefore connects the usefulness of the seeding exponent to specific properties of the underlying clustering.

For mixtures of Gaussian distributions with comparable variances and a constant number of mixing weights, any fixed α greater than two gives a constant-factor approximation. The authors also obtain guarantees for arbitrary mixing weights. Lower bounds show that the dependence on concentration and relative standard deviation is tight, while experiments validate the influence of the analyzed parameters.
icml-2024-analyzing-d-seeding-for-k-mean.tldr: The paper explains when using seeding exponents above two gives strong expected guarantees for ordinary k-means clustering.

paragraphs: The paper investigates language-model internals through geometry. It derives closed-form descriptions of the intrinsic dimension available to multi-head attention embeddings and of the regions and affine mappings formed by feedforward layers. These descriptions turn aspects of internal representations into mathematical objects that can be analyzed directly.

The authors use this analysis in two applications. First, they show that informed prompt manipulation can control embedding dimension and bypass protection from reinforcement learning with human feedback. Second, they construct interpretable geometric features that can be extracted from pretrained language models and used to represent properties of their inputs.

The extracted features help detect toxicity and distinguish different types of toxic content. Together, these findings connect exact structural analysis with both a model vulnerability and a detection task. The contribution is therefore more than a description of representation geometry: it demonstrates that geometric quantities can guide practical interventions and provide useful signals for understanding language-model inputs.
icml-2024-characterizing-large-language-.tldr: Exact descriptions of language-model geometry support interpretable toxicity detection and reveal a way to bypass RLHF protection through prompt manipulation.

paragraphs: Cluster deletion asks how few edges can be removed from a graph so that the remaining groups are cliques, meaning that every pair of vertices within a group is connected. Finding the optimum is NP-hard. The paper develops better guarantees and simpler procedures for approximate solutions, with applications including biological and social networks.

The first contribution is a tighter analysis of two existing algorithms. Their approximation factors improve from four to three, strengthening the guarantee on how many edges they delete relative to an optimal solution. The authors also show how to remove randomness from both methods through a simple greedy rule: choose a maximum-degree vertex in an auxiliary graph and form a cluster around it.

One of the algorithms involves a linear program. The final contribution is a purely combinatorial approach for handling that component, with better scalability in theory and practice. Together, the results improve the mathematical guarantee while making the underlying computation simpler and more scalable.
icml-2024-combinatorial-approximations-f.tldr: Sharper analysis, simple derandomization, and a combinatorial approach improve the guarantees and scalability of cluster-deletion algorithms.

paragraphs: Unsupervised reinforcement learning aims to acquire behaviors before a task-specific reward is available. The paper identifies a tension in existing approaches: empowerment-based discovery can produce static skills, while maximizing exploration alone emphasizes visiting states without necessarily producing useful behaviors. The proposed framework seeks both broad exploration and distinct skills.

It organizes an ensemble of skills around state prototypes that define clustered regions. Each skill explores its own region locally, while the ensemble collectively expands overall state coverage. Constraints relate each skill’s occupancy distribution—the states it tends to visit—to its intended cluster, encouraging the skills to remain distinguishable.

The authors provide theoretical analysis of state entropy and the resulting skill distributions. Experiments on challenging tasks show well-explored skill ensembles and better performance on various downstream tasks than previous methods. The approach matters because it gives exploration an internal organization: broad coverage is distributed across identifiable behaviors that can later be useful when a concrete task is introduced.
icml-2024-constrained-ensemble-explorati.tldr: An ensemble of skills explores separate constrained state regions, combining broad coverage with distinguishable behaviors that improve downstream task performance.

paragraphs: Adversarial purification tries to remove malicious changes from an input before a classifier uses it. Diffusion models are promising for this task because they can generate and reconstruct data, but guidance designed for other generation goals may not suit purification. This paper develops guidance specifically for recovering useful signal from attacked inputs.

The authors analyze both stages of diffusion from a feature-learning perspective. They theoretically derive an appropriate amount of noise for the forward process. For the reverse process, their analysis suggests that guidance from a contrastive loss helps move the evolving representation toward the signal direction. The resulting method combines calibrated Gaussian noise addition with gradients of that contrastive loss.

Experiments cover CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, traffic-sign recognition, and ImageNet with ResNet and WideResNet classifiers. The authors report large improvements over most of the adversarial-training and purification methods considered. The findings support coordinating noise selection and reverse-process guidance around the purification objective, with the empirical claim applying to the evaluated settings.
icml-2024-diffusion-models-demand-contra.tldr: Contrastive guidance and theoretically motivated noise selection improve diffusion-based adversarial purification across the evaluated image-classification settings.

paragraphs: Disentangled representations aim to separate different factors of variation in data. Many existing methods encourage latent variables to have a factorized joint distribution. This paper proposes TopDis, which instead uses the topological structure of data manifolds to guide how a representation separates those factors.

TopDis adds a differentiable loss that measures topological similarity across manifold traversals at multiple scales. This provides an additional training signal based on the structure encountered as a representation varies. The method is unsupervised, so it does not require labels identifying the underlying factors, and the authors report that the loss also works when those factors are correlated.

Experiments show improved MIG, FactorVAE, SAP, and DCI disentanglement scores relative to state-of-the-art results while maintaining reconstruction quality. The authors also demonstrate using the loss to identify disentangled directions in an already trained GAN. These results suggest that topological structure can help organize latent variation without requiring the usual emphasis on statistically independent factors.
icml-2024-disentanglement-learning-via-t.tldr: TopDis uses a differentiable multiscale topological loss to improve unsupervised disentanglement while preserving reconstruction quality, including with correlated factors.

paragraphs: A metric embedding represents graph vertices as points in another space while approximately preserving distances between them. This paper studies how to maintain such a representation in ℓp space as edge weights increase in a weighted, undirected graph. The challenge is to keep the representation useful throughout the sequence of changes.

The authors give a randomized dynamic algorithm with expected distortion O(log² n), where n is the number of vertices. Distortion measures the multiplicative discrepancy between distances in the embedding and in the graph. Their total update-time guarantee combines an almost-linear dependence on the initial edge count with the number of updates and logarithmic factors involving graph size and maximum edge weight.

The paper also establishes a contrasting limitation for fully dynamic graphs, which permit edge insertions and deletions: no algorithm can explicitly maintain a low-distortion embedding with high probability in that regime. The results therefore provide a positive guarantee for weight increases and a separate impossibility result for the broader update setting.
icml-2024-dynamic-metric-embedding-into-.tldr: A dynamic algorithm maintains graph embeddings with O(log² n) expected distortion under edge-weight increases, alongside a fully dynamic impossibility result.

paragraphs: Multi-task learning shares knowledge across tasks, but their training signals can conflict. A step that benefits one task may interfere with progress on another, making it difficult to distribute improvement fairly. This paper treats that conflict as a resource-allocation problem inspired by communication networks.

The authors formulate training as utility maximization over decreases in task losses. Different fairness measurements specify how those improvements should be distributed. Their proposed objective, FairGrad, supports flexible emphasis on particular tasks and comes with a theoretical convergence guarantee. Fairness here concerns the allocation of optimization progress across tasks.

Across supervised-learning and reinforcement-learning benchmarks, the authors report state-of-the-art performance among gradient-manipulation methods. They also incorporate α-fairness into the loss functions of other multi-task methods and find significant empirical improvements. The results suggest that an explicit choice about how to share progress can be useful both as a new optimization objective and as a modification to existing approaches.
icml-2024-fair-resource-allocation-in-mu.tldr: FairGrad allocates loss improvements across tasks using fairness-based utility maximization, with a convergence guarantee and strong benchmark performance.

paragraphs: Reconstructing inputs is an appealing way to learn representations, but accurately reproducing data need not prioritize the features useful for perception. This paper identifies a mismatch: reconstruction directs model capacity toward data subspaces that explain observed variance, even when those subspaces provide relatively little information for a perception task.

A TinyImagenet example illustrates the distinction. Images projected onto a leading subspace explaining 90% of pixel variance yield 45% supervised test accuracy, whereas a bottom subspace accounting for only 20% yields 55%. The authors also find that reconstruction learns perception-relevant features late, contributing to the need for long training schedules.

The paper proves that denoising can alleviate this mismatch for some noise strategies, including masking. Choosing an effective strategy without knowing the downstream perception task remains challenging. The authors also provide a way to identify strategies that are never beneficial regardless of the perception task, giving additive Gaussian noise as an example. The key implication is that the corruption strategy matters to what denoising learns.
icml-2024-how-learning-by-reconstruction.tldr: Reconstruction can prioritize high-variance features over useful perceptual ones, while denoising with certain noise strategies can alleviate that mismatch.

paragraphs: This paper examines whether the image supplied to a vision-language model can redirect its behavior during inference. The authors discover image hijacks: adversarial images that influence generated responses. Their results show that an input image can become a means of controlling behavior beyond the ordinary visual content it represents.

They introduce Behaviour Matching, a general algorithm for training these images. A derived method, Prompt Matching, trains an image to reproduce behavior associated with an arbitrary user-defined text prompt. It can use a generic dataset unrelated to that prompt, making the desired behavior separate from the dataset used to train the hijack.

The authors evaluate four attack goals against LLaVA: chosen outputs, disclosure of context-window information, overriding safety training, and acceptance of false statements. Every attack type exceeds an 80% success rate in their study. The attacks are automated and use small image perturbations. These findings establish a substantial vulnerability in the evaluated model, without establishing the same success rate for every vision-language system.
icml-2024-image-hijacks-adversarial-imag.tldr: Small adversarial image perturbations redirect LLaVA’s behavior, with over 80% success for each of four evaluated attack types.

paragraphs: A language model can mislead users by expressing confidence in incorrect claims. This paper defines linguistic calibration through the decisions its text supports: a model is calibrated when users can turn its long-form responses into calibrated probabilistic predictions. The focus is therefore on how uncertainty language informs downstream judgments.

The training procedure has two stages. Supervised fine-tuning first teaches the model to include confidence statements in extended answers. Reinforcement learning then rewards responses that help a user give calibrated answers to related questions. This connects the training objective to the probability judgments readers make after interpreting the generated text.

Applied to Llama 2 7B, the method produces significantly better calibration than strong factuality-focused fine-tuning baselines at comparable accuracy in automated and human evaluations. The improvement also carries over to scientific and biomedical questions and a held-out biography task. These findings support training uncertainty communication end to end through its effect on users’ predictions, rather than treating confidence wording as an isolated output feature.
icml-2024-linguistic-calibration-of-long.tldr: Training long-form answers around users’ downstream probability judgments improves linguistic calibration while maintaining accuracy comparable to factuality baselines.

paragraphs: Video transformers often process only short time spans because their quadratic complexity makes longer contexts expensive. Extending those contexts can introduce additional computational and conceptual complexity. This paper proposes adapting existing pretrained video transformers so they can use information retained from earlier portions of a video.

The method, MC-ViT, fine-tunes a transformer to attend to memories derived non-parametrically from past activations. Redundancy reduction consolidates those memories, allowing the model to draw on a more distant past. This connects current processing to earlier internal representations while reusing an existing pretrained video encoder.

The authors report strong scaling when learning from longer videos and new state-of-the-art results on EgoSchema, Perception Test, and Diving48. MC-ViT also outperforms methods with orders of magnitude more parameters. These findings indicate that retaining and consolidating past activations can be an effective route to longer-context video understanding, and that access to relevant history can deliver gains without relying on a much larger model.
icml-2024-memory-consolidation-enables-l.tldr: MC-ViT extends pretrained video transformers with consolidated memories of past activations, achieving leading results on three long-context video benchmarks.

paragraphs: The paper asks how much computation is fundamentally required to minimize an average of n component functions. It assumes that the full objective satisfies the Polyak–Łojasiewicz condition and that the components satisfy mean-squared smoothness. The ratio of the smoothness and PL parameters defines the condition number κ.

Under these assumptions, any gradient method needs at least Ω(n + κ√n log(1/ε)) incremental first-order oracle calls to reach error ε. Such calls access first-order information about individual components. The bound nearly matches the performance guarantees of the best-known methods, showing that their computational requirements are close to the fundamental lower limit.

The authors also analyze a connected network in which different agents hold different component functions. They establish separate lower bounds for communication rounds, total time, and local oracle calls, exposing the roles of network spectral gap and communication cost. Finally, they propose a decentralized first-order method that nearly matches these bounds in expectation, linking the impossibility results to an achievable algorithm.
icml-2024-on-the-complexity-of-finite-su.tldr: The paper establishes nearly tight computational and communication lower bounds for smooth finite-sum PL optimization and a decentralized method that nearly attains them.

paragraphs: Switching dynamical systems describe sequences whose hidden dynamics can change between regimes. This paper studies identifiability: whether the latent variables and mappings of such a model can be determined from the observed data, subject to specified ambiguities. That question matters when hidden states are intended to carry an interpretable meaning.

The authors first prove identifiability for Markov switching models, which often provide the prior for continuous latent variables. Their identification conditions concern first-order Markov structures with nonlinear Gaussian transition distributions. They then establish identifiability of latent variables and nonlinear mappings in switching dynamical systems up to affine transformations, retaining that specific ambiguity rather than claiming unique recovery.

The paper also develops estimation algorithms for the identifiable models. Empirical studies demonstrate their practicality for segmenting high-dimensional sequences, including videos, and use identifiable Markov switching models for regime-dependent causal discovery in climate data. The contribution combines conditional recovery guarantees with methods and applications that make those guarantees relevant to sequential data analysis.
icml-2024-on-the-identifiability-of-swit.tldr: Under stated identification conditions, switching dynamical systems permit recovery of latent variables and nonlinear mappings up to affine transformations.

paragraphs: Some hard optimization problems admit strong approximation schemes when their instances are dense. The paper starts from a classical scheme that gives polynomial-time solutions within a 1−ε approximation factor for any positive ε, covering a family that includes Max-CUT and Max-k-SAT. It asks how predictions can make this approach faster.

The authors extend the scheme using only a logarithmic number of one-bit predictions. Their learning-augmented framework explicitly tracks how approximation quality depends on prediction error. It seeks consistency when predictions are accurate, smooth degradation as their errors increase, and robustness when predictions are unreliable.

They provide algorithms with these properties for dense instances of several optimization problems. The central contribution is the combination of faster approximation and restrained use of predictions: useful assistance comes from a small amount of predicted information. The scope remains dense instances of the covered problem family, and the guarantees are designed to account for prediction errors rather than assuming that the supplied advice is always correct.
icml-2024-parsimonious-learning-augmente.tldr: A logarithmic number of one-bit predictions speeds approximation schemes for dense hard problems while preserving guarantees that account for prediction error.

paragraphs: Federated learning uses local training steps to reduce communication, but their benefits under differing client data are not fully explained by optimization analyses. Motivated by experiments in which Local SGD learns more distinguishing features than parallel SGD, this paper investigates how local updates affect the features a neural network acquires.

The authors introduce a federated data model with a new form of heterogeneity. Within that model, a convolutional neural network trained by gradient descent with global updates misses some pattern-related features, whereas local updates learn all features in polynomial time. This difference yields better generalization for local training in the proposed setting.

Under a different parameter setting, they also prove that local gradient descent followed by a single model-averaging step can learn all features and generalize well across clients. Experiments on real-world data support the benefit of local steps for test accuracy. The theoretical contribution is a conditional feature-learning explanation for those benefits, rather than a universal claim that local updates always outperform global ones.
icml-2024-provable-benefits-of-local-ste.tldr: In a proposed heterogeneous federated data model, local updates learn features missed by global updates and thereby improve CNN generalization.

paragraphs: Comparing graphs without vertex attributes requires a measure of similarity based on structure. The paper introduces QBMK, a quantum-based matching kernel that compares aligned vertices through quantum Shannon entropies obtained using a continuous-time quantum walk. This combines explicit vertex correspondence with structural information associated with each matched vertex.

The theoretical analysis addresses two shortcomings of existing kernels. R-convolution kernels can neglect which structural parts correspond across graphs, while vertex-matching kernels can neglect structural differences between vertices they align. QBMK is designed to account for both correspondence and difference. Its entropy-based representation can also capture local and global structural characteristics simultaneously.

Experiments on standard graph datasets show that QBMK can outperform state-of-the-art graph kernels and graph deep-learning approaches. The contribution is therefore a way to make graph similarity sensitive both to which vertices are matched and to the structures around them. The reported empirical advantage supports that combination in the evaluated datasets rather than establishing a universal ranking of graph-comparison methods.
icml-2024-qbmk-quantum-based-matching-ke.tldr: QBMK compares aligned vertices using quantum-walk entropies to capture structural correspondence, differences, and both local and global graph information.

paragraphs: Some neural-network properties concern several executions together. Examples include robustness against a perturbation shared across inputs and certified worst-case Hamming distance for binary-string classifications. Verifying such properties requires reasoning about relationships among executions, rather than analyzing each input-output computation independently.

The paper identifies a source of imprecision in existing verification approaches. Most focus on single executions, and even some relational methods capture only linear dependencies between inputs. They leave unused the dependencies that arise between hidden-layer outputs across executions. Those internal relationships can provide additional information for bounding the network’s possible behavior.

The authors introduce RACoon, a scalable verifier that uses cross-execution dependencies throughout all layers of a network. It achieves substantially greater precision than state-of-the-art baselines across varied datasets, networks, and relational properties. The significance is that verification can become more informative by preserving relationships inside the computation, rather than discarding them after the inputs. This targets a specific weakness in how existing methods represent multiple related executions.
icml-2024-relational-dnn-verification-wi.tldr: RACoon improves relational neural-network verification by using dependencies between multiple executions at every network layer.

paragraphs: Self-attention adjusts which tokens receive emphasis, but the relationship between that localization and model behavior is difficult to explain. Two failure modes seem to point in different directions: rank collapse makes token representations too similar, while entropy collapse produces strongly nonuniform attention and can make learning more prone to plateaus.

The paper studies localization through the eigenspectrum of query-key parameter matrices. Rather than describing attention only by the probabilities it assigns to tokens, the authors connect its behavior to a spectral property of the parameters that generate those probabilities. They find that small variance in this eigenspectrum leads to localized attention.

The analysis further shows that small eigenspectrum variance prevents both rank collapse and entropy collapse, improving expressivity and trainability. This connects apparently conflicting accounts through a common parameter-level characterization. The finding matters because localization and the two kinds of collapse need not be treated as interchangeable: the spectral view identifies a setting in which attention localizes while avoiding both problematic behaviors.
icml-2024-self-attention-networks-locali.tldr: Small query-key eigenspectrum variance leads to localized attention while preventing both rank and entropy collapse.

paragraphs: The paper asks whether transformers can carry out the reasoning steps of graph algorithms, beyond showing that they perform well on examples. It studies a looped transformer architecture equipped with additional attention heads that interact with the graph. Repeated execution provides the setting for simulating algorithmic steps.

Through explicit constructions, the authors prove that this architecture can simulate Dijkstra’s shortest-path algorithm, breadth-first search, depth-first search, and Kosaraju’s strongly connected-components algorithm. It can also simulate multiple algorithms simultaneously. The parameter count stays fixed as the input graph grows, so larger graphs do not require a separately enlarged parameter set.

The theoretical simulation applies to arbitrary graph sizes, but the authors identify a finite-precision limit in their solution. They additionally establish Turing completeness at constant width when the extra graph-interacting attention heads are available. These are expressiveness results about what carefully constructed networks can implement; the fixed parameter count and finite-precision qualification are both important to interpreting that computational capability.
icml-2024-simulation-of-graph-algorithms.tldr: Constructed looped transformers simulate several graph algorithms with graph-size-independent parameter counts, subject to a finite-precision limitation.

paragraphs: Formal verification aims to establish guarantees about neural-network behavior, including robustness against adversarial changes. Its practical difficulty is partly a tradeoff between scale and precision. To handle large computations, verifiers use approximations that can be too loose to establish whether the desired property holds, leaving the analysis inconclusive.

This paper proposes modifying a trained network to make it more amenable to verification. Its post-training optimization framework balances preservation of prediction performance against verification-friendliness. The resulting Verification-Friendly Neural Networks, or VNNs, are intended to retain useful predictive behavior while making formal analysis more effective.

The authors report prediction performance comparable to the original networks and time-efficient verification that establishes robustness for more VNNs than their original counterparts. The contribution therefore concerns both the network and the proof process: changing the trained model can improve the ability to certify its behavior. The claim is that more robustness properties can be established for the resulting networks, rather than that every transformed network is automatically robust.
icml-2024-vnn-verification-friendly-neur.tldr: Post-training optimization makes neural networks easier to verify while preserving comparable prediction performance and enabling more time-efficient robustness certificates.
